doc.title: Cascadu interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, November 15, 2019

chapter: Spirit, roots and the music's meaning
title: Conch horn solo, Mayaro memories and learning on the street
summary: He tells of a conch horn solo with T.K. Blue, its memories and maroon history, and says many musicians learned by living the music.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Yeah and this is what, I mean, this is how I interact in the music you know. I remember doing a concert recently and I hadn’t brought out my conch horns in a long time. And I decided just to work with it and something just told me just to work with it. We were doing a concert with T.K. Blue called Motherland Connections, right? And when it came time for the solo, instead of doing a conga solo I just knew, something just guided, pick up the conch horn. And I did a solo on the conch horn. And that horn I remember as a little boy, my family would get away every summer and we would go spend some time on a beach that my mom and dad really, really loved called Mayaro, which is on the southeast coast of Trinidad, and we would rent a place and we would stay there for the whole summer. But the entire thing about that was that on the morning, early in the morning you would hear the conch horn blowing to call the fisherman to come to go out to fish. And then from the boat and from the land you would hear these conch horns going back and forth when the fisherman were coming back in because what they were doing is they were calling the villagers to come and help pull in the seine nets. Right? And so we would get up and we would go and we would be hauling in nets, and you know everybody is pulling seine and everything, and tons of fish coming in. I mean that was life. Later on as I grew up and I learned more, you know, that horn was actually a symbol of the freedom and the power and another level of communication among the maroon slaves, especially the maroons in the Coptic country of Jamaica. They called it abhang and they use the conch horn and another animal horn to signal if the infiltrators were coming close by and they would set up these calls all over to alert the other communities, the other maroon communities, the runaway slaves, you know, that the Spaniards or the British or the French or whoever, that they were coming, that people were coming. So I got up and I took this conch horn solo you know. And it just came out of my heart you know. And it was well received. I didn’t expect it at all, I just went, you know, I just went with the moment. So this is what happens. There’s a color. There’s something in the music when you live that close to the earth you know, that it’s not cerebral. It’s not something that okay this is where this goes etcetera. It’s in response to what’s going on. It’s in response to what’s happening in the music. And I think for all these people that, all these guys man, all the guys who play this music and jazz and you know, the Brazilian jazz and the roots of jazz — when you sit down and you talk to them it’s not their academic study that made them the musicians that they are. Yes it helped them, no doubt. But there are a lot of them that never even went to school and they

picked up, they got their chops on the street. They got their chops on the stage. They got their chops, you know, on the road you know? And it became something that they lived. It became something that gave them — that fed their spirit. Their body might have deteriorated but their spirit and their soul was being fed by something that we can’t put our finger on.

Exactly. And I have experienced that with people like, these photos we are looking at taken by Milt Hinton and that generation, somehow in talking to them and just sitting next to them you felt better afterwards, like they were passing on whatever it is that we can’t nail down, but it is something that gets passed on.
